prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the rare case where a continuum-model band-structure calculation (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) predicted a controllable flat band, and a decisive experiment (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) then found correlated insulators and superconductivity. From my own field it is a concrete discovery about nature rather than a method or an instrument: bandwidth, filling and interactions can be tuned in a single device, and the same logic has since been extended to many moire systems. Theory and experiment are cleanly separable, so a three-name split is defensible. Seven years of independent reproduction by many groups, and the follow-on discoveries the platform has produced, show that the core finding is stable even though some interpretation is still open.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is timing and credit. The pairing mechanism and the nature of several correlated phases are still debated, twist-angle disorder limits how much of the detailed phase diagram is reproducible, and the first author of the 2018 experiments, Yuan Cao, and parallel moire work by the Dean, Young and Kim groups are not in the credited names. A committee that waits for a settled interpretation would rank topological insulators or circuit QED, both about two decades old, ahead of this. I accept that this is a fair reason to hold back, and that my own ranking leans on being close to the electronic-structure side of the problem.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first on a clear, independently confirmed concept, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene seventh because the interpretation of superconductivity is unsettled and a final prize may be early.
responses.response: I agree the interpretation is unsettled and that the clocks are more mature and more precisely defined. But the committee does not need a settled pairing mechanism to credit the discovery: the achievement is the prediction of the magic-angle flat band and the observation of correlated states in it, and both are secure. I rank the clocks sixth mainly because I cannot judge priority within metrology; I take Lindroth's point that Katori and Ye form a clean two-name case, and I would not object if the committee preferred it, but I do not think maturity alone should place it above a discovery that opened a new class of quantum matter.

responses.point: Mehlig places circuit QED first and twisted bilayer graphene sixth, citing the field's youth and that Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, is not among the credited names.
responses.response: The attribution concern is serious and I share it: a prize for the experiment that omits the first author invites criticism. I would still argue that the Nobel tradition credits the group leader who conceived and directed the programme, as with Jarillo-Herrero here, and that the theory-plus-experiment structure is unusually clean for a moire prize. Where I disagree is on prematurity: the flat-band correlated regime has been reproduced in many laboratories, so the open question is the mechanism, not whether the effect exists. I concede that if the committee wants to avoid any doubt about the experimental credit, circuit QED is a safer choice.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean, mature, field-defining architecture, and notes that it follows naturally from the 2025 circuit-based prize, with only a mild risk of looking too close.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is mature and cleanly attributed, and I list it as an alternative. My reservation is the one Johansson himself raises: coming right after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, a second superconducting-circuit award risks looking like the same community rewarded twice, whereas moire materials would broaden the prize into a different part of condensed matter. I also note the attribution question about Girvin, who co-authored the founding proposal and is not in the credited names, which leaves the circuit QED trio less tidy than the opening ballots suggest.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for opening a new observational window, and places twisted bilayer graphene fourth with the superconductivity mechanism still contested and recognition somewhat early.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce that the superconductivity mechanism is contested and that the field is young. I disagree that this makes the central discovery early, since flat-band correlated insulators have been confirmed by many groups. On IceCube, I cannot judge detector and background issues as he can, and I accept that the diffuse flux is solid; but the source-level evidence rests on few objects, and I would want the committee to hear whether that makes the achievement complete or still ongoing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unresolved pairing mechanism as a reason to wait on twisted bilayer graphene.
Whether the experimental credit can be defended without Yuan Cao and the other 2018 co-authors, and how the Dean, Young and Kim groups' parallel moire work should be weighed.
Whether circuit QED looks too close to the 2025 prize, which would change my ranking between B024 and B016.
I cannot independently verify priority details in metrology, neutrino astronomy or cosmology, where I am not a specialist.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work in electronic-structure theory and correlated electrons is adjacent to moire materials and to the topological-insulator candidate, so I note that field proximity, but my profile documents no personal or institutional connection to any credited name.
